one_liner: Research home of ipnsort and driftsort, Rust's standard sorts since 1.81; ipnsort beats libstdc++ and libc++ std::sort on 10k u64.
what_it_does: The repository holds a sort test suite (Ord, panic and observation safety), a Criterion benchmark suite that calls vendored Rust, C and C++ sorts through a C ABI, fuzz harnesses, and the ipnsort source. ipnsort (unstable) and driftsort (stable, by Orson Peters and Lukas Bergdoll) replaced slice::sort_unstable and slice::sort in rust-lang/rust PR 124032 and shipped in Rust 1.81.0 (2024-09-05), so Rust users get them by calling the usual slice methods. Neither is published as a standalone crate (crates.io has no ipnsort or driftsort crate, and the driftsort repo says it is not intended as a standalone library); C and C++ code has no API to call.
how_it_is_fast: ipnsort keeps the pdqsort skeleton (quicksort with ancestor-pivot equal-element filtering, so K distinct values cost O(N log K)) but adds a single-pass already-sorted/reversed scan, glidesort's recursive sqrt(N) median pivot, a branchless cyclic Lomuto partition for small types, sorting-network plus bidirectional-merge small-sorts, and a branchless heapsort fallback at depth 2*log2(N). It aims at instruction-level parallelism, not SIMD, so it stays generic over Ord and user comparators. driftsort combines glidesort-style run detection and lazy merging with a branchless stable quicksort partition and a branchless merge. The author puts the gap down to older C++ std implementations, not to the language: C++ pdqsort (144.4 us on random) matches the old pdqsort-based Rust sort (136.9 us).
when_to_use: Rust code that sorts integer-like or small Copy keys: slice::sort_unstable is already ipnsort on Rust 1.81+, with the largest measured gains on low-cardinality (random_d20: 24.3 us vs 136.5/97.6) and Zipfian inputs.
Generic sorts with user comparators where a buggy Ord must not cause memory unsafety: ipnsort is Ord-, panic- and observation-safe and usually panics on a detected strict-weak-order violation.
Sorting already ascending or descending data: ipnsort does N-1 comparisons (2.07 us vs 49.3 us for libstdc++ std::sort on 10k ascending u64).
As a design reference for a C or C++ port, or when choosing a C++ replacement: the same plot shows C++ pdqsort and C crumsort recover most of the gap over std::sort.
when_not_to_use: Inside C++ code: there is no C/C++ interface, so you would need Rust FFI or a port; pdqsort, crumsort or vqsort in C/C++ are the practical substitutes.

Append-then-sort (random_s95): ipnsort ties libc++ std::sort (83.4 vs 84.2 us) and is about 5x slower than crumsort (16.9 us), because it scans 95% of the input before giving up on the already-sorted check.

Maximum integer throughput: the authors list SIMD sorts (vqsort with AVX2+ and Clang), radix or counting sorts for small keys, and multithreading for multi-millisecond sorts as faster options outside its design goals.
Code whose Ord is inconsistent: since Rust 1.81 the new sorts may panic on non-total orders where the old ones silently returned unsorted data.
Memory-tight stable sorts: driftsort allocates an N-element buffer up to 8 MB and N/2 beyond; there is no published driftsort-versus-C++ stable_sort measurement in this repo.

integration.form: module (Rust standard library slice::sort / sort_unstable since 1.81.0); research copy is a path crate (ipnsort/) in this repo, not on crates.io
integration.dependencies: none (ipnsort is no_std without alloc; driftsort needs alloc for its buffer)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.81.0 for the std versions; the research repo builds on nightly (specialization in src/ffi_util.rs; the benchmark used rustc 1.75.0-nightly 2023-10-03)
integration.platforms: any Rust target; no architecture-specific code (designed and tuned for rustc with LLVM only)
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded in-place sort of a &mut slice; no internal parallelism
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: drop-in only as Rust's own slice::sort_unstable/sort; not callable from C++ in place of std::sort without FFI or a port

gotchas: Harness checked, no flaw found: the C++ rows call std::sort/std::stable_sort with the default operator< once per sort through extern "C" (src/cpp/cpp_std_sort.cpp), Criterion iter_batched_ref regenerates input each iteration (switched from iter_batched in commit e698b65 after issue #13, before this 2023-10 run), and the thread is pinned to one core; no contestant used -march=native. The libstdc++ variant uses the cc crate's default C++ compiler (gcc 13.2.1), the libc++ variant clang 16.0.6 with -stdlib=libc++.

The baselines are old: LLVM 16 libc++ std::sort predates the bitsetsort-derived rewrite (LLVM 17), which the writeup calls untested; only hot-cache 10k u64 on one Zen 3 box was measured, and the ipnsort tested (commit 757478b) predates the code merged into std in June 2024.
Doc mismatch: the writeup says random_d20 is 0..=20, but benches/bench.rs builds it with random_uniform(len, 0..20).

Stable half: the plot shows the 2022 Rust merge sort, not driftsort; it loses to libstdc++ std::stable_sort on random_d20 and random_p5 and to libc++ on random, random_d20 and random_z1. glidesort, driftsort's ancestor, beats both C++ stable sorts on every pattern except random_p5 against libstdc++ (74.1 vs 69.8 us).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: This is the primary source behind the sibling 'Rust slice::sort (LangArena Sort::Self) vs C++ std::sort' entry (driftsort, 0.41 s vs 0.982 s). That sibling supplies the third-party C++ comparison of driftsort that this repo lacks, while this entry adds per-pattern ipnsort-versus-std::sort numbers with published flags. Prefer it over the Zig std.sort.pdq sibling when the code is Rust; neither helps a C++ codebase without a port.
verified_claims_summary: On 10k u64 with a hot cache (Ryzen 9 5900X, rustc 1.75.0-nightly with thin LTO, C++ at -O3 -std=c++20), ipnsort sorted random input in 77.0 us vs 297.6 us for libstdc++ std::sort (gcc 13.2.1) and 265.1 us for libc++ std::sort (clang 16.0.6). Across seven patterns it was 2.2x to 23.8x faster than libstdc++ and 1.01x to 4.0x faster than libc++ (plot values, ratios derived from page data). driftsort was not part of the run.
status_note: Research repo is active (last commit 2026-03-02, Apache-2.0); the production code lives in rust-lang/rust and is maintained there, so it is copyable in principle but in practice usable only from Rust 1.81+.
